raw_text:
### Introduction and Epidemiology
Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative, progressive, and historically underdiagnosed cardiomyopathy characterized by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardial interstitium [1,2]. These deposits lead to progressive wall thickening, ventricular stiffening, and restrictive physiology [3,4]. Although numerous proteins can theoretically form amyloid, the vast majority of clinically significant cases are classified into two primary etiologies: light-chain amyloidosis (AL-CA) and transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR-CM) [3,5]. AL-CA is a hematologic condition caused by a clonal population of plasma cells producing unstable monoclonal immunoglobulin free light chains [2,5]. In contrast, ATTR-CM stems from the misfolding of the liver-synthesized transport protein transthyretin [1,4]. ATTR-CM is further divided into hereditary or variant ATTR (hATTR/ATTRv), inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion due to mutations in the *TTR* gene, and wild-type ATTR (wtATTR), an age-related systemic disease without a genetic mutation [4]. Modern epidemiological studies have debunked the notion that wtATTR is an ultra-rare disease, demonstrating that it represents an underappreciated etiology of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) in the elderly [1,6].

### Clinical Presentation and Diagnostic "Red Flags"
Early recognition of cardiac amyloidosis remains a major challenge [6,7]. Patients frequently undergo years of diagnostic delays and see multiple specialists before receiving an accurate diagnosis [6]. The disease typically presents as progressive heart failure accompanied by systemic "red flags" that should alert the clinician [7,8]. For wtATTR, musculoskeletal manifestations often precede cardiac symptoms by up to a decade [7,9]. These include bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, trigger finger, and spontaneous distal biceps tendon rupture [9,10]. In both AL and ATTR subtypes, advanced disease is marked by severe dyspnea, autonomic dysfunction (e.g., orthostatic hypotension), conduction system disease, and high-dose loop diuretic intolerance [7,10].

### Diagnostic Imaging: Electrocardiography, Echocardiography, and Cardiac MRI
The diagnostic workup often begins with non-invasive imaging. Low QRS voltage on electrocardiogram discordant with the degree of left ventricular wall thickness is a classic clue, although its absence does not rule out the disease [11]. Transthoracic echocardiography characteristically reveals concentric left ventricular wall thickening (>12 mm) with preserved ejection fraction until late stages [12]. Speckle-tracking echocardiography is highly sensitive, demonstrating a pathognomonic "apical sparing" pattern of global longitudinal strain (GLS), where myocardial contractility is preserved at the apex but severely reduced at the base [11,12].

Multi-societal consensus guidelines have standardized these findings to streamline clinical suspicion [13,14]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging has emerged as an invaluable tool for tissue characterization [15]. Typical CMR features of CA include diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement (LGE), alongside marked elevations in native T1 relaxation times and myocardial extracellular volume (ECV) fraction [15,16]. Both LGE and ECV quantification correlate strongly with the myocardial amyloid burden and serve as powerful independent predictors of all-cause mortality [17,18].

### Scintigraphy and the Non-Biopsy Diagnosis
A revolutionary milestone in CA management was the establishment of a highly specific non-biopsy diagnostic algorithm [3]. Nuclear scintigraphy utilizing technetium-labeled bone-seeking radiotracers, such as 99mTc-pyrophosphate (PYP) or 99mTc-3,3-diphosphono-1,2-propanodicarboxylic acid (DPD), demonstrates intense myocardial avidity in ATTR-CA [19,20]. Under the validated diagnostic paradigm, the presence of Grade 2 or 3 myocardial radiotracer uptake on planar and SPECT imaging, coupled with the absolute exclusion of a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia, is 100% specific for ATTR-CA, bypassing the historical requirement for endomyocardial biopsy [3,20]. Crucially, to rule out AL-CA—which represents a medical emergency—every patient undergoing scintigraphy must be screened for monoclonal proteins [21]. This screening must include a serum free light chain (sFLC) assay along with serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE) [21,22].

### Therapeutic Paradigms
Therapeutic strategies have advanced rapidly, transitioning from purely supportive care to highly effective disease-modifying therapies. In AL-CA, the primary goal is rapid elimination of the clone producing the amyloidogenic light chains [23]. The current front-line standard of care is the combination of the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab with cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (Dara-CyBorD), which has significantly improved hematological and cardiac organ response rates [23,24]. Eligible, lower-risk patients may also undergo high-dose melphalan chemotherapy followed by autologous stem cell transplantation [24,25].

For ATTR-CA, management centers on TTR tetramer stabilization or gene silencing. The TTR stabilizer tafamidis was the first drug shown to reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations in patients with both wild-type and hereditary ATTR-CA in the landmark ATTR-ACT trial [26]. More recently, the novel high-affinity TTR stabilizer acoramidis achieved highly potent tetramer stabilization and met its primary hierarchical endpoint with favorable survival and hospitalization profiles in the phase 3 ATTRibute-CM trial [27]. In parallel, TTR gene-silencing agents, which suppress TTR synthesis in the liver, have transformed care. The small interfering RNA (siRNA) patisiran and the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen first proved highly effective in mitigating neuropathy in hATTR [28,29]. Subsequently, in the landmark phase 3 HELIOS-B trial, the long-acting subcutaneously administered siRNA vutrisiran demonstrated profound clinical efficacy, significantly reducing the composite of all-cause mortality and recurrent cardiovascular events in patients with ATTR-CA [30].

These rapid clinical, diagnostic, and therapeutic breakthroughs have transformed cardiac amyloidosis from a once neglected, rapidly fatal condition into a highly treatable disease, underscoring the vital importance of early detection.
